entityDossier.whatItIs: A peer-reviewed review article, "Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics," by Garry P. Nolan, Jacques F. Vallee, Sizun Jiang and Larry G. Lemke, published in Elsevier's Progress in Aerospace Sciences, Volume 128, January 2022, article 100788 (online 9 December 2021), DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2021.100788. Its first half reviews mass-spectrometry and imaging methods for characterizing unknown solids; its second half applies them to a preserved sample, designated CB_JV-1, from the 17 December 1977 molten-metal fall at Council Bluffs, Iowa. It is the first materials-analysis paper on a UAP-associated sample to appear in a mainstream aerospace journal.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This paper is the methodological hinge of the entire material-evidence question. It puts on the record, in a journal that describes itself as invitation-only and that is read by the aerospace engineering community, a replicable protocol for exactly the task a legacy exploitation program would have been performing in secret for decades: determining whether a recovered solid was manufactured, by whom, and by what process. Its lead author, Garry Nolan, is a Stanford professor of pathology whose analytical lab work brought him into contact with the contractor-adjacent UAP community; its second author, Jacques Vallee, holds the sample catalogue that has been the reference set for physical-trace UFO cases since the 1960s. The paper cites, on page 3, one of the Defense Intelligence Reference Documents produced under the DIA-funded Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program (AAWSAP) - Maxim Tsoi's "Metallic Spintronics" (2010) - which drags a government UAP-program artifact into the open Elsevier literature and into a citation graph that can be followed. Finally, the paper's actual result is the inconvenient one: isotope ratios consistent with terrestrial norms, but an inhomogeneity pattern the authors say would not be expected to form naturally and that they cannot source to any identified industrial process. That is the shape of an evidentiary problem, not a claim of proof - which is what makes it usable.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Council Bluffs event is one of the very few physical-trace cases in the UFO record with a same-night, multi-agency chain of custody. At approximately 1945 CST on 17 December 1977, two residents of Council Bluffs, Iowa, watched a red luminous mass descend near the northern city limits. When they reached the site they found ground covered by molten metal glowing red-orange and igniting grass. Police and fire personnel were on scene within roughly fifteen minutes and all of them saw the mass, which they estimated at 35 to 55 pounds. Investigators at the time ruled out re-entering space debris, falling aircraft material, a meteorite (there was no crater), and a hoax. Two of the eleven witnesses described a round object hovering in the sky edged with red blinking lights. Vallee took possession of a fragment. Forty-four years later Nolan's Stanford laboratory - which had developed Multiplexed Ion Beam Imaging (MIBI), a mass-spectrometric imaging technique built for tissue but capable of resolving a much broader isotope range than the 1978-era instruments - ran it again.

The result was not what either camp wanted. The paper reports that all isotopic ratios were similar between the samples and did not show statistically significant deviations from expected terrestrial normal, with one exception involving 57Fe for which the authors themselves offer a conventional explanation. In other words: the sample is made of Earth atoms. What the paper does not do is stop there. The elemental map shows local homogeneity inside individual measured grains but pronounced inhomogeneity across subsamples, which the authors read as incomplete mixing - the fingerprint of a process, not a natural formation. Their published summary of the Council Bluffs material is that it shows no evidence of having been engineered or designed, would not be expected to form naturally, and has unusual inhomogeneity. The origin, handling history and delivery mechanism remain unidentified.

The hostile reading of the paper is worth cataloguing because it is specific and it is on the record. The most detailed public critique, a long-form analysis at Metabunk, argues that the four most abundant elements identified in the paper's Figure 9 - aluminium, silicon, iron and magnesium - are the 3rd, 2nd, 4th and 7th most abundant elements in Earth's crust and are all consistent with a thermite or improvised-thermite reaction; that the MIBI-SIMS configuration used cannot detect oxygen, which would be the discriminating element for a redox reaction; that two of five subsamples returned compromised ion counts; that the paper's citation of Southall and Oberly's 1979 paper on airborne superconducting generators does not support the liquid-metal and novel-propulsion inferences drawn from it; and that roughly 350 words are reused near-verbatim from Vallee's own 1998 paper "Physical Analyses in Ten Cases of Unexplained Aerial Objects with Material Samples" without being marked as reused. None of these critiques have produced a retraction, and none of them contradict the isotopic finding. They are, for an analyst, a checklist of what a replication attempt has to close out.

The reason this paper matters to a board about a concealed program is structural rather than evidentiary. Every version of the legacy-program hypothesis reduces, eventually, to a claim about custody of physical material. Every official denial reduces to a claim about the absence of such material. Both claims are testable by exactly the instruments described here, and only by them. The Nolan-Vallee paper is therefore the open-literature specification of the test that the government has consistently declined to submit its holdings to - and, notably, the government has since begun performing a shadow version of the same test on its own terms. AARO's FY2024 annual report to Congress states plainly that Oak Ridge National Laboratory "provided analysis for a material claimed to be from a UAP" and that AARO S&T, in coordination with ORNL, wrote and posted a materials-analysis report on its website, with supplemental data promised. That is the same workflow, run inside the fence, with the sample provenance and the raw data controlled by the party with the strongest institutional interest in the answer.

The analyst-facing question the paper leaves open is not whether CB_JV-1 is alien. The authors expressly refuse that framing, writing that the objective is to provide data in an open-source manner so that others might replicate the analytic approaches or derive a testable hypothesis for how such materials are deposited. The question is who else has run this protocol, on what, and where those results went. Nolan has stated publicly that he has analysed other samples; the paper itself notes further analyses in progress. The gap between the published Council Bluffs work and whatever else has passed through that instrument is one of the more tractable research targets on this board.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Roswell Report: Case Closed is a 231-page official United States Air Force publication authored by Capt. James McAndrew of the Secretary of the Air Force Declassification and Review Team at the Pentagon, printed by the U.S. Government Printing Office and released on 24 June 1997. It is the follow-on to the 1994-95 Air Force report The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert by Col. Richard L. Weaver and then-1st Lt. James McAndrew. Its purpose is to account for the reports of 'alien bodies' that the 1995 report had left unaddressed.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is a denial artifact, and it is catalogued here as evidence about the denier rather than about Roswell. It is dated, signed, congressionally provoked, and printed at government expense, which makes it the most attributable statement the Air Force has ever made on the subject - and its internal logic reveals precisely which claims the Air Force judged it could not leave standing. Its core mechanism is temporal: it asserts that Air Force activities spread across many years have been consolidated by witnesses into two or three days in July 1947, and that UFO proponents mis-dated the 'alien' observations "in some instances by more than a decade." It was released on the 50th anniversary of the Kenneth Arnold sighting, a date choice that is itself a communications decision. And it is the direct product of a General Accounting Office audit initiated at the request of a sitting member of Congress, which means the Air Force wrote it under external compulsion rather than voluntarily - the only such instance in the pre-2017 record. The GAO audit that produced it also established, on the record, that Roswell Army Air Field's administrative records for March 1945 through December 1949 and its outgoing messages for October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, with no indication of by whom or under what authority.
entityDossier.narrative:
The sequence matters more than the content. In 1993 Rep. Steven H. Schiff (R-New Mexico) began asking the Department of Defense about Roswell and, dissatisfied, referred the matter to the General Accounting Office. The GAO tasking forced the Office of the Secretary of the Air Force into an exhaustive records search that concluded in July 1994 and produced roughly 1,000 pages of material, published in 1995 as The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert. Secretary of the Air Force Sheila E. Widnall released interviewees from any security obligations that might have restricted their statements. The 1995 report's answer was Project Mogul: a then-classified balloon-borne acoustic sensor program whose train components, it said, accounted for the debris. Notably, the Mogul records that carried the explanatory weight had never been classified at all; other Mogul records had been declassified en masse under Executive Order 11652, signed by President Nixon on 6 March 1972.

Mogul explained debris. It did not explain bodies. Case Closed exists to close that gap, and its four stated conclusions are worth reading as a list of the specific narrative threads the Air Force needed cut. First, that Air Force activities occurring over a period of many years "have been consolidated and are now represented to have occurred in two or three days in July 1947." Second, that "'Aliens' observed in the New Mexico desert were probably anthropomorphic test dummies that were carried aloft by U.S. Air Force high altitude balloons for scientific research." Third, that the reports of military units arriving shortly after a crash to retrieve a saucer and its crew "were actually accurate descriptions of Air Force personnel engaged in anthropomorphic dummy recovery operations." Fourth, that claims of bodies at the Roswell Army Air Field hospital were most likely a conflation of a 1956 KC-97 accident in which eleven airmen were killed and a 1959 manned balloon mishap in which two pilots were injured.

Read as an intelligence product, this is a substitution table. Each item on the left is a witness-reported element of a retrieval operation - non-human bodies, a cordon, a convoy, a hospital, injured or dead personnel - and each item on the right is a real, documented, unclassified Air Force activity that produces the same observable. The Air Force is not arguing that nothing happened. It is arguing that everything happened, repeatedly, over fifteen years, and that the witnesses stacked it. The named substitutes are Projects High Dive and Excelsior, the Holloman-based dummy-drop and high-altitude-bailout programs; the dummies are identified in the report's own figures as Alderson Laboratories and 'Sierra Sam' type anthropomorphic dummies. Appendix B is a set of signed sworn statements from in-person interviews, including Col. Charles A. Coltman Jr. (USAF Medical Corps, retired), Col. Dan D. Fulgham (retired) - the pilot injured in the 1959 balloon mishap - and Bernard D. Gildenberg, the Holloman balloon engineer.

The report's own framing gives away its function. It states that its findings run "Contrary to allegations that the Air Force has engaged in a cover-up and possesses dark secrets involving the Roswell claims." That sentence is not a finding; it is a rebuttal, and it identifies the audience. The title itself - Case Closed - is a declaration of jurisdiction over when an inquiry ends, which is the specific authority a service branch does not actually have with respect to Congress.

What the report does not address is the record-destruction finding that emerged from the same GAO audit. GAO/NSIAD-95-187, released 28 July 1995, reported that RAAF administrative records from March 1945 through December 1949 and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 had been destroyed, and that the document disposition form did not indicate what organization or person destroyed them, when, or under what authority. The GAO also found that Army Air Force regulations in 1947 required air accident reports to be maintained permanently, that four such accidents were reported in New Mexico in July 1947 - all after 8 July, the date the RAAF public information office announced recovery of a flying disc - and that USAF officials told GAO there was no requirement to report the crash of a balloon.

Case Closed has since been absorbed into the current official narrative without qualification. AARO's Historical Record Report Volume 1, published 8 March 2024, cites it approvingly, restating the dummy explanation and the 1956/1959 hospital conflation verbatim as established results. That continuity is the point: the 1997 denial is not a historical curiosity, it is a live load-bearing element of the 2024 denial.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Fiscal Year 2024 Consolidated Annual Report on Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena, produced by the Department of Defense All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office (AARO) with an information cut-off of 1 June 2024 and released 14 November 2024. It is submitted to Congress under a statutory requirement at 50 U.S.C. 3373(k) and covers UAP reports from 1 May 2023 to 1 June 2024 plus all prior-period reports not previously reported. It was drafted in coordination with more than two dozen named organisations including ODNI, the Service intelligence centres, NRO, NGA, NSA, DIA, FBI, NCIS, DoE, NASA, the NNSA and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: AARO is not a neutral authority here; it is the office the Department created to be the answer to the question, and this report is the instrument by which it discharges its obligation to Congress. What makes it load-bearing is not its denials but the specific admissions embedded in them. Section IV.G is headed "AARO Possesses No Data to Indicate the Capture or Exploitation of UAP" and its entire body is a single sentence stating that AARO is working with mission partners "to formalize a process in the event UAP materiel is captured" - meaning that as of mid-2024 no such process existed anywhere the office could see. Section VI.C confirms that Oak Ridge National Laboratory analysed "a material claimed to be from a UAP." Section VI.D confirms AARO posted historical documents on KONA BLUE, a prospective and unapproved Special Access Program that interviewees described as a DHS compartment to cover up "the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" And the report concedes that 444 of the 757 reports lacked sufficient data for any analysis and that AARO received zero UAP reporting through national GEOINT, SIGINT or MASINT platforms during the entire period - the national technical means that would find a concealed program were not pointed at the problem at all.
entityDossier.narrative:
Read as a compliance document, the FY2024 report is a study in what a statutory reporting requirement can and cannot compel. 50 U.S.C. 3373(k)(1)(B) enumerates roughly fifteen mandatory content items, and the report walks them in order: events in period, events out of period, analysis by intelligence discipline, incidents over restricted airspace, threats, foreign attribution, breakthrough foreign capability, allied consultation, capture-or-exploitation efforts, health effects, nuclear-asset association, NNSA and NRC consultation, designated line organisations, and a summary of authorised reporting. The statute is well drafted. The answers are mostly negative, and the negatives are the interesting part.

The numbers: 757 reports received, of which 485 occurred in the reporting period and 272 occurred in 2021-2022 but were only reported now. Cumulative holdings as of 24 October 2024 were 1,652 reports. Of the 757, 392 - more than half - came from the FAA, and consisted of the entire FAA UAP reporting log since June 2021. By domain: 708 air, 49 space, zero maritime, zero transmedium; and AARO notes that none of the space-domain reports came from space-based sensors, all being pilot or ground-observer accounts of objects estimated above 100 kilometres. AARO resolved 49 cases in-period, recommended 243 more for closure, judged 21 to merit further analysis by intelligence-community and science-and-technology partners, and consigned 444 to an 'Active Archive' for lack of data. By publication, the office reported 118 resolved and a further 174 finalised, all to prosaic objects.

The key sentence for anyone tracking concealment is buried in Section III.B: "During the reporting period, AARO did not receive any UAP reports collected through national GEOINT, SIGINT, or MASINT platforms." Every input was pilot report, post-mission full-motion video, or FAA log. AARO can search IC databases case-by-case, but nothing was tasked. Whatever else the report establishes, it establishes that the collection architecture of the United States was not being used to answer this question during the period covered.

The second key passage is the nuclear-infrastructure section. AARO received eighteen reports from the NNSA Administrator and the NRC Chairman regarding incidents near U.S. nuclear infrastructure, weapons and launch sites, all of which those agencies categorised as unmanned aircraft systems. Two involved incursions of 53 minutes and one hour 57 minutes. On 3 August 2023 security at the D.C. Cook Nuclear Power Plant recovered a crashed UAS and turned it over to Berrien County, Michigan local law enforcement; AARO states flatly that it "has no further information about the crashed UAS." A recovered object over a nuclear facility left the federal system entirely and the office statutorily charged with anomaly resolution never got it back. Separately, the BWXT Fuel Cycle Facility in Lynchburg, Virginia experienced UAS overflights on six consecutive nights, 10-15 October 2023.

The third is the authorities language. AARO asserts it "is authorized by law to receive all UAP related information including any classified national security information involving military intelligence or intelligence related activities at all levels of classification, regardless of any restrictive access controls, special access controls, or compartmented special access programs," with "no restriction on AARO receiving any past or present UAP-related information, regardless of the organizational affiliation of the original classification authority." This is the exact authority whose absence is the subject of the Wilson-Davis memo - a Deputy Director of DIA being told by a contractor committee that his tickets and statutory authority were not sufficient. The FY2024 report asserts the authority exists. It does not report ever having exercised it against a waived or unacknowledged SAP, nor does it report a single instance of an access denial.

The science-and-technology section names the partner set: Oak Ridge National Laboratory for physics-relevant case analysis and the UAP-material analysis; the Air Force Research Laboratory for propulsion, stealth and sensing assessments; the Georgia Tech Research Institute, which built the GREMLIN sensor architecture that demonstrated functionality in a March 2024 test and was slated for a 90-day pattern-of-life collection "at a site of national security"; MIT Lincoln Laboratory, building prototype processing to recover objects currently filtered out of FAA and National Weather Service radar; and NASA as focal point for academic and open-source work. That is a real, funded, technically competent architecture, and its existence should be weighed against the report's own admission that the office cannot resolve most of its caseload.

Finally, the strategic communications section records that AARO posted historical documents relating to KONA BLUE, characterising it as "a Prospective and not approved Special Access Program that was brought to AARO's attention by interviewees who claimed that it was a sensitive Department of Homeland Security compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics.'" entityDossier.narrative:
The document must be handled as three separable things: an artifact with a physical history, a set of assertions about 1997, and a contested attribution. Keeping them separate is what makes it usable.

As an artifact, its most consequential fact is institutional. The Internet Archive copy of the annotated memo cites, as its provenance, the congressional document HHRG-117-IG05-20220517-SD001 posted at congress.gov under the 17 May 2022 hearing of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Subcommittee on Counterterrorism, Counterintelligence and Counterproliferation - the first open congressional UAP hearing in over fifty years. Reporting indicates Rep. Mike Gallagher raised the document with the Pentagon witnesses and obtained unanimous consent to enter it into the record. Whatever its authenticity, it is now a document in a congressional hearing file, and its assertions are therefore assertions Congress has formally received and not adjudicated.

As a set of assertions, the notes describe a search rather than a revelation. Wilson, then Deputy Director of DIA and Assistant JCS J-2, is depicted as acting after an April 1997 Pentagon conference-room briefing given by Steven Greer, Cmdr. Willard Miller and Edgar Mitchell, at which Adm. Mike Crawford and Wilson's superior Lt. Gen. Patrick Hughes were present. Wilson and Miller then spoke privately for two hours about, in the memo's phrasing, UFOs, MJ-12, Roswell, crashed UFOs and alien bodies. Wilson is described as already knowing of intelligence on US military and foreign government close encounters. Over roughly forty-five days he made calls, was pointed by Maj. Gen. Ward and by Perry toward the records groups in OUSD(A&T), located what he describes as a special projects record group that did not belong to the usual SAP divisions as organised by Perry in 1994, and read the index abstracts. He is described as being told by Kostelnik that program security costs ran two to three times the program budget and at times six to seven times core budget, that Perry had wanted an investigation of that ratio and was told to drop it, and that Judith Daly explained the discrepancy as a records-keeping artifact of cumulative versus annual reporting.

What follows is the part that is genuinely novel in the UFO literature, because it is not about a craft. It is about jurisdiction. Wilson is described as making three calls to the program manager, one a conference call with a security director and a corporate attorney, and then flying out ten days later to meet the same three in a secure vault. They call themselves "the watch committee" or gatekeepers, and explain that they formed after an earlier audit investigation nearly exposed them, following which a formal agreement was struck with SAPOC establishing special access criteria administered by the contractor committee rather than by the government, such that no USG personnel gain access unless the contractor's criteria are met "irregardless of the tickets and position USG personnel possessed." Wilson's regulatory and statutory authority as Deputy Director DIA is declared not relevant to their program. He is shown a bigot list several pages long, dated 1990 and updated 1993, mostly program employees, civilians, with a handful of recognisable Pentagon names from OUSD(A&T), one from another department, and one at the NSC who was a Pentagon SES employee. No politicians. No White House. No Congress.

Only then does the substance appear, and it is brief: the program manager states they are not a weapons, intelligence, special operations or logistics program; that they are a reverse engineering program; that something was recovered years ago; that they have an intact craft they believe could fly; that it did not come from overseas and could not have; that they did not know where it was from; that it was "technology that was not of this Earth - not made by man - not by human hands"; that progress had been agonisingly slow with painful lack of outside collaboration; and that the bigot-list workforce ran about 400 to 800 people varying with funding. On Roswell, Holloman, MJ-12 and Zamora and Bentwaters, they declined to discuss. Wilson threatened to escalate to SAPOC, did so, and the Senior Review Group sustained the contractor twice, told him to drop it, and - per the memo - the chairman warned he would not see the DIA director promotion, would get early retirement, and would lose one or two stars. In January 1998 Wilson is described as raising his June 1997 meetings with the new Under Secretary Jacques Gansler, who had somehow been briefed, and who said: "UFOs are real, so-called 'alien abductions' not real."

As a contested attribution, the record is unambiguous on one side and silent on the other. Wilson has denied it directly, telling a reporter it is all fiction, that he would not know Eric Davis if he walked in, and that he did not sit in a car with him in Las Vegas for an hour; he says he told both a Senate staffer and AARO that Davis is making it up. Davis has declined to comment publicly on the document since it appeared. Individuals identified in the memo as arranging the meeting are reported to have denied knowing Wilson. And AARO's own Historical Record Report Volume 1, the government's most extensive published treatment of exactly these allegations, does not contain the name Wilson anywhere in its 1,500-plus lines of text - it disposes of the entire category by asserting that claims involving specific people, locations, tests and documents are inaccurate and largely the product of circular reporting, without engaging this document at all. A critical handling note: the widely circulated PDF is an annotated version, and the marginal identification of Lockheed Martin as the unnamed contractor is the anonymous annotator's inference, not anything attributed to Wilson in the notes.

claims.text: AFOSI was founded on 1 August 1948 at the suggestion of Congress to consolidate Air Force investigative activities; Secretary of the Air Force W. Stuart Symington appointed Special Agent Joseph Carroll, a senior FBI official and assistant to Director J. Edgar Hoover, as first AFOSI commander, and Carroll later became the first Director of the Defense Intelligence Agency (1961).

On 9 August 1980 security guards at the Manzano Weapons Storage Area adjacent to Kirtland AFB reported a bright light descending in a restricted area; a report was filed with AFOSI at Kirtland and the incident was investigated by Special Agent Richard Doty.

Richard C. Doty, a former AFOSI counterintelligence special agent, has publicly acknowledged participating in disinformation operations directed at UFO researchers, including Albuquerque physicist Paul Bennewitz, during the late 1970s and 1980s; Doty and Linda Moulton Howe both state they met at Kirtland AFB in April 1983.

AFOSI remains inside the current UAP reporting architecture: the May 2023 Joint Staff GENADMIN, as described in AARO's FY2024 annual report, directs Combatant Commands and Services to report all UAP incidents, incursions and engagements to Joint Operations Centers, Service Watch Centers and respective counterintelligence elements within 96 hours, and AFMD 39 makes AFOSI the sole counterintelligence element of the Department of the Air Force.

entityDossier.denialPosture: AFOSI's institutional posture, expressed through its command historian in the 6 August 2020 osi.af.mil feature, is endorsement of the Project Blue Book conclusions - no indication of threats to U.S. national security, no evidence of unexplained advanced technology, no evidence that the reports were extraterrestrial vehicles, across 12,618 sightings of which 701 remained unidentified - while conceding those results "were controversial and remain so to this day." AFOSI has published no institutional statement acknowledging, explaining or disavowing the Doty disinformation operations.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Galileo Project for the Systematic Scientific Search for Evidence of Extraterrestrial Technological Artifacts is a Harvard-hosted, cross-institutional research programme launched in July 2021 and co-founded by Avi Loeb, the Frank B. Baird Jr. Professor of Science at Harvard, and Frank Laukien, chairman, president and CEO of the scientific instrument manufacturer Bruker Corporation. It operates three branches: the study of interstellar objects near Earth, the search for unidentified aerial phenomena using multimodal ground-based observatories, and the study of interstellar meteors. It is funded entirely by private donation.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Galileo is the control experiment for this entire board. Every version of the legacy-program hypothesis and every official denial of it reduce to claims about physical evidence held under classification. The only structural way to break that is an independent, uncleared, publishing instrument capable of producing calibrated data on the same phenomena - data that is not subject to prepublication classification review because it was never collected on government money or on government sensors. Galileo is the first serious institutional attempt to build one, and its funding structure is the mechanism: $1.755 million raised in the first two weeks from named private donors, which means its outputs go to arXiv rather than to a DOPSR queue. Its director also co-authored a March 2023 draft paper with Sean Kirkpatrick, the sitting Director of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office - the only documented instance of a joint technical product between the Pentagon's UAP office and an independent academic programme. And its IM1 interstellar meteor work is the most instructive public failure mode on the board: a physical-recovery campaign that produced material, published it, and could not establish a chain from the material to the event, generating a citation war that maps precisely onto the epistemics of the whole subject.
entityDossier.narrative:
Loeb's framing paper, "Overview of the Galileo Project," was posted to arXiv on 2 August 2022 as arXiv:2209.02479 and published in a special issue of the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation in 2023. Its abstract describes the project as "the first systematic scientific research program in search for potential astro-archaeological artifacts or remnants of extraterrestrial technological civilizations (ETCs) or potentially active equipment near Earth," and characterises the approach as taking a path not taken and conceivably picking low-hanging fruit. That is a statement about method, and the method is the point: Galileo's premise is that the subject has been starved of instrumented, calibrated, continuous data, not of anecdotes.

The UAP branch built to that premise. Wesley Watters and colleagues published "The Scientific Investigation of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) Using Multimodal Ground-Based Observatories" in the Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation, volume 12, article 2340006 (2023), laying out the sensor architecture: synchronised optical, infrared, radio, magnetometric and acoustic channels producing a continuous census of everything above an observation site, so that anomaly is defined by exclusion from a measured baseline rather than by the surprise of an observer. The first instrument came online at Harvard. Commissioning results for the all-sky infrared camera array were posted as arXiv:2411.07956, and a system architecture paper followed as arXiv:2506.00125. Loeb has publicly discussed commissioning data covering roughly half a million objects. No Galileo detection has been shown to be non-human technology, and the project has not claimed otherwise.

The interstellar meteor branch is where the project collided with the discipline. CNEOS 2014-01-08, designated IM1, is a bolide detected over the western Pacific whose inferred velocity implied a hyperbolic, interstellar trajectory. In summer 2023 Galileo mounted an ocean expedition off Papua New Guinea, dragging a magnetic sled across a roughly ten-kilometre region around the fireball localisation across twenty-six runs and recovering approximately 700 sub-millimetre spherules. Loeb and colleagues reported that a subset had a distinctive composition rich in beryllium, lanthanum and uranium - the 'BeLaU' type - which they argued was inconsistent with solar-system materials. The chemical classification work was eventually published in Chemical Geology (2024), with the preprint at arXiv:2401.09882.

The response was immediate and formal, and it is worth cataloguing precisely because it is the model of how a materials claim gets adjudicated in the open. Steve Desch and Alan Jackson published a direct critique, arXiv:2311.07699, arguing among other things that the spherules plot on or extremely near a terrestrial fractionation line and that a body entering at the assumed IM1 velocity would have been essentially vaporised, so that recovered iron spherules cannot be attributed to that event. A separate paper, arXiv:2403.05161, proposed the BeLaU signature as microtektites of terrestrial laterites. Most damaging to the localisation, Fernando and colleagues published "Seismic and acoustic signals from the 2014 'interstellar meteor'" in Geophysical Journal International, volume 238, issue 2 (2024), concluding that the seismic signal used to pin the impact site changed direction over time in a way that matched a road running past the seismometer - a truck, not a bolide. Galileo replied with "Peak-Brightness Localization of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) Fireball," arXiv:2403.07696, arguing that the search region was set by the NASA/JPL CNEOS localisation box - 11.112 km on a side, centred at 1.3 degrees south, 147.6 degrees east - and not by the seismic data at all.

Whichever way that dispute resolves, its structure is the finding. A privately funded team recovered candidate material, published composition data, and could not establish provenance linking material to event; independent groups published falsifying analyses within months; the original team responded in the same channel. This is exactly the adjudication process that has never been available for any material alleged to be in government custody, and the contrast is the argument. The Nolan-Vallee 2022 paper faces the same problem from the other direction - a sample with a documented same-night recovery but a forty-four-year custody gap.

The most direct institutional connection on the board is the Loeb-Kirkpatrick paper. Dated 7 March 2023 and titled "Physical Constraints on Unidentified Aerial Phenomena," it derives physical constraints on interpretations of highly manoeuvrable UAP from standard physics and known forms of matter and radiation, and it is co-authored by the serving Director of AARO. The draft circulated publicly, drew criticism from multiple directions, and was never formally issued as an AARO product. It nonetheless establishes that the Pentagon's UAP office and Galileo were in direct technical collaboration during Kirkpatrick's tenure, which bears on how one reads AARO's later categorical statements and on what data, if any, moved in either direction.

For an analyst, Galileo's value is threefold. It produces a public, timestamped, instrumented baseline that any future disclosure has to be consistent with. Its funding graph - Eugene Jhong, Vinny Jain, Teddy Jones, Eric Keto, the Laukien Science Foundation, Joerg Laukien, William A. Linton, Adnan Sen, the Brinson Foundation - identifies the private capital willing to underwrite the question outside the appropriations system. And through Laukien and Bruker it sits one step from the mass-spectrometry instrument industry whose products define what any materials claim, government or otherwise, can actually be tested with.

claims.text: Loeb, A. (on behalf of the Galileo Project, Harvard University), "Overview of the Galileo Project," arXiv:2209.02479, submitted 2 August 2022, published in Journal of Astronomical Instrumentation (Special Issue), 2023, describes the project as "the first systematic scientific research program in search for potential astro-archaeological artifacts or remnants of extraterrestrial technological civilizations (ETCs) or potentially active equipment near Earth."
The Galileo Project was launched in July 2021, co-founded by Avi Loeb of Harvard and Frank Laukien, chairman, president and CEO of Bruker Corporation.

The project received donations totalling $1.755 million in its first two weeks; named donors include Eugene Jhong, Vinny Jain, Teddy Jones, Eric Keto, the Laukien Science Foundation, Joerg Laukien, William A. Linton, Adnan Sen and The Brinson Foundation. It receives no government funding.

Commissioning results for the Galileo Project's all-sky infrared camera array were published as "Commissioning An All-Sky Infrared Camera Array for Detection Of Airborne Objects," arXiv:2411.07956.
The observatory system design was published as "Galileo Project Observatory Class System Architecture," arXiv:2506.00125.

In 2023 the Galileo Project conducted an ocean expedition near Papua New Guinea targeting the site of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) bolide, recovering approximately 700 sub-millimetre spherules across 26 magnetic-sled runs criss-crossing a roughly 10-kilometre region around the fireball location.

Loeb and colleagues reported a subset of the recovered spherules with a distinctive beryllium-, lanthanum- and uranium-rich ('BeLaU') composition claimed to be of extrasolar origin; the chemical classification work was published as "Chemical classification of spherules recovered from the Pacific Ocean site of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) bolide," Chemical Geology (2024), preprint arXiv:2401.09882.

Steve Desch and Alan Jackson published a formal critique, arXiv:2311.07699, "Critique of arXiv submission 2308.15623, 'Discovery of Spherules of Likely Extrasolar Composition in the Pacific Ocean Site of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) Bolide', by A. A competing terrestrial explanation for the BeLaU signature was published as "Be,La,U-rich spherules as microtektites of terrestrial laterites: What goes up must come down," arXiv:2403.05161.

Fernando et al., "Seismic and acoustic signals from the 2014 'interstellar meteor'," Geophysical Journal International 238(2):1027 (2024), concluded that the seismic signal used to localise the IM1 impact site changed direction over time in a way matching a road running past the seismometer, i.e. a truck rather than a bolide.

The Galileo Project responded with "Peak-Brightness Localization of the CNEOS 2014-01-08 (IM1) Fireball," arXiv:2403.07696, arguing the search region was set by the NASA/JPL CNEOS localisation box measuring 11.112 km on a side centred at 1.3 degrees south, 147.6 degrees east, and not by the seismic data.

entityDossier.denialPosture: Galileo issues no denials; it is the party against which official denial is directed. Its own posture is one of null results honestly reported - no Galileo observation has been shown to be non-human technology, and the project has repeatedly declined to assert probabilities. That posture is itself evidentially useful, because it establishes that the project's later claims, if any, would not be the product of a group predisposed to affirm.
